--- title: "Dependent data" description: "Visits to one site share its water and seabed, so a survey's rows are worth fewer independent stations than their number. Resampling whole sites instead of single stations measures how many fewer." order: 3 categories: [assumptions, spatial-temporal] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Rows that share conditions are not separate evidence Two observations are independent when one says nothing about the other beyond what their inputs say. **Dependent data** share conditions, so one does say something about the other. [The coastal survey](../02-marine-data/the-coastal-survey.qmd#repeat-visits-to-the-same-sites-are-not-independent) found that its rows come from far fewer monitoring sites, and called treating repeat visits as separate observations pseudo-replication; that is why [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) keeps each site's rows together. This page measures what the survey's rows are worth as evidence. The same problem appears wherever one unit is sampled several times: | What is repeated | What the rows share | The unit to count | | --- | --- | --- | | Visits to a fixed station | Depth, seabed, local water | The station | | Sub-samples from one grab | The grab | The grab | | Fish measured from one haul | The haul, the gear, the day | The haul | | Readings down one CTD cast | The water column | The cast | ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Resampling whole groups measures the effective sample size A [bootstrap sample](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd#a-random-forest-averages-trees-grown-on-resampled-data) draws rows at random with replacement, as many as the data has. Drawing many and computing an average in each shows how far that average moves from one sample of the survey to the next. Drawing single rows treats every row as independent. Drawing whole sites, each with all its visits, treats only the sites as independent. If drawing whole sites spreads the average wider, the visits to a site were partly repeating each other. The difference converts into a number of stations. An average's spread shrinks with the square root of the number of independent observations, so a spread $k$ times wider means the rows are worth $k^2$ times fewer: the **effective sample size**. ::: {.diagram} ![Resampling stations draws single visits; resampling sites draws each site with all its visits.](img/resample-sites.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. The survey, sites with repeat visits: four sites, A to D, each a box holding three to five visits drawn as dots in the site's colour; visits to one site share its water and seabed, so they tend to agree. Resample stations, draw one row at a time: sixteen draws of a single visit each, with the colours mixed, so every row counts as separate evidence. Resample sites, draw whole sites: four draws of a whole site with all its visits, one site drawn twice and one not at all, so only sites count as separate evidence. A note says if resampling sites spreads an estimate wider, the visits were repeating each other."} ::: ## Worked example The whole survey is used, since nothing on this page is a final score. Five hundred bootstrap samples are drawn by station, and five hundred by site. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() resamples <- list( "Single stations" = bootstraps(survey, times = 500), "Whole sites" = group_bootstraps(survey, group = site_id, times = 500) ) # how far the average of some values moves from one resample to the next, # for each way of resampling spread_of <- function(values) { map_dbl(resamples, \(r) { sd(map_dbl(r$splits, \(s) mean(values[as.integer(s)]))) }) } tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| sites| |--------:|-----:| | 800| 160|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() rng = np.random.default_rng(123) levels = {"Single stations": "station_id", "Whole sites": "site_id"} def resamples(column, times=500): """Row numbers of each bootstrap sample that draws whole groups.""" rows_of = list(survey.groupby(column).indices.values()) samples = [] for _ in range(times): drawn = rng.integers(0, len(rows_of), len(rows_of)) samples.append(np.concatenate([rows_of[i] for i in drawn])) return samples samples = {level: resamples(column) for level, column in levels.items()} def spread_of(values): values = np.asarray(values) return pd.Series({level: np.std([values[rows].mean() for rows in drawn], ddof=1) for level, drawn in samples.items()}) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [survey["site_id"].nunique()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | sites | |-----------:|--------:| | 800 | 160 | ::: ::: ::: ### Visits to one site repeat each other's catch The estimate is the simplest one: the average catch per station, in each of the bootstrap samples. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} catch_spread <- tibble(resampled = names(resamples), spread = spread_of(survey$abundance)) |> mutate(wider = spread / first(spread), worth = nrow(survey) / wider^2) catch_spread |> mutate(across(spread:wider, \(x) round(x, 2)), worth = round(worth)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|resampled | spread| wider| worth| |:---------------|------:|-----:|-----:| |Single stations | 0.17| 1.00| 800| |Whole sites | 0.22| 1.31| 468|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} catch_spread = spread_of(survey["abundance"]).rename("spread").to_frame() catch_spread["wider"] = catch_spread["spread"] / catch_spread["spread"].iloc[0] catch_spread["worth"] = len(survey) / catch_spread["wider"] ** 2 catch_spread.round({"spread": 2, "wider": 2, "worth": 0}).reset_index( names="resampled") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | resampled | spread | wider | worth | |:----------------|---------:|--------:|--------:| | Single stations | 0.17 | 1 | 800 | | Whole sites | 0.23 | 1.38 | 417 | ::: ::: ::: The 800 stations come from only 160 sites. Drawing whole sites spreads the average catch 1.31 times wider than drawing single stations, so for this estimate the stations are worth about 470 independent ones. An interval for the average built as if all 800 were independent would be too narrow: the survey would look surer than it is. A site's depth and seabed stay much the same from one visit to the next, so a deep muddy site is rich every time it is sampled and a shallow rocky one poor every time. Its visits partly repeat each other. A model's score has the same problem. A held-out visit predicted by a model fitted to the same site's other visits has been helped by them, and looks easier than a new site would be. That is why the course scores models on whole sites held out, as [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) and [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) did. ## Neighbouring sites and years share conditions too Neighbouring sites share a water mass and a stretch of seabed, and samples from one year share its weather. [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) holds out whole areas of the map and whole years for them. Resampling by group needs enough groups, and it needs to know which group each row came from. Datasets often lose the grab, haul or cast a row came from when they are summarised, and once that column is gone the repeats cannot be found. Keep the identifier of the unit sampled, and report both numbers: how many rows, and how many sites. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Visits to one site share its depth, seabed and water: they are **dependent data**, and are not fully separate evidence. - Resampling whole sites instead of single stations measures the shortfall: a spread $k$ times wider means the rows are worth $k^2$ times fewer, the **effective sample size**. For the average catch, the 800 stations were worth about 470. - A model must be scored on whole sites held out, or the site's other visits help it. Keep the identifier of every unit sampled. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Measure what the stations are worth for the average depth, `survey$depth_m`, which changes little between visits to a site. How does the answer compare with the number of sites? 2. Do the same for the average temperature, which changes with the season; add `na.rm = TRUE` to the `mean()` inside `spread_of()` (`np.nanmean()` in Python), since a few temperatures are missing. Are the stations worth more or fewer for temperature than for depth, and why?
